A holistic workforce acquisition and development plan for DOW energy systems could mitigate this risk. 3.4 Performance Under Extreme Conditions Just as diesel fuel can gel in cold temperatures, the performance of some advanced energy technologies can degrade under different weather conditions (e.g., batteries in extreme cold and PV panels in extreme heat), which can impact DOW costs, planning, and readiness. Moreover, having different systems that perform variably across different environments complicates logistics, as it may require additional spare parts, specialized maintenance knowledge, or redundant systems to ensure reliability. This increases the logistical burden on deployed forces, reduces standardization across units, and can strain sustainment operations in contested or resource-limited environments. DOW missions often require operations in harsher conditions than the commercial sector, so its energy technologies must reliably perform under extreme temperatures and withstand shock and vibration (FCAB 2021). While the Army’s Cold Regions Research and Engineering Laboratory tests some technologies, one interviewee specializing in Arctic issues noted that DOW typically tests technologies in moderate climates, leaving greater uncertainty around choosing advanced energy technologies for extreme environments. For example, extreme cold temperatures can impair battery performance and lifetime (Walsh et al. 2024). Studies have shown that battery EV range can drop by more than 40% in typical cold conditions (around 20°F), while internal combustion engine vehicles experience an approximate 10% range drop in the cold (Walsh et al. 2024). Li-ion batteries with carbonaceous anodes, the dominant type used in vehicles, are generally known for their poor performance at sub-zero (oC) temperatures, including the inability to be charged quickly. In hot climates (such as in Arizona and coastal/saltwater environments), Li-ion batteries used in EVs and stationary storage experience accelerated degradation, leading to more frequent replacements (Pesaran, Santhanagopalan, and Kim 2013). Further, certain components of solar PV systems can be less durable when exposed to extreme heat, humidity, or hail; and solar panels in regions prone to heatwaves can experience efficiency declines (Masterson 2022). Operational testing in extreme physical conditions and allowing for higher rates of inoperability in operational plans would help mitigate this risk. 3.5 Power Density Some advanced energy technologies have lower power densities than legacy alternatives and require more surface area or volume to produce an equivalent amount of power (Van Zalk and Behrens 2018). This could hinder DOW’s ability to rapidly deploy or sustain forces in contested or austere environments where space, concealment, and mobility are critical. For example, power density is a key shortcoming of Li-ion batteries, which provide significantly less energy per unit of weight and volume than conventional fuels (Shaffer 2024).
